title: 1st Grade Addition Word Problems: The 3 Story Types (+ Free Quiz)
meta_title: 1st Grade Addition Word Problems + Free Quiz
meta_desc: The three kinds of 1st grade addition word problems a six-year-old meets, a read-underline-solve-check method, worked examples within 20 and a free quiz.
excerpt: Almost every addition story a first-grader meets is one of three kinds. Once a child can name the type, the sum writes itself. Here are the three, a four-step method, and a quick quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Read this one to a six-year-old: ‘Aarav had 7 marbles. His sister gave him 5 more. How many does he have now?’ Most children can add 7 and 5 on a good day. What trips them up is the words in between — deciding whether the story even wants an addition. That gap, between the arithmetic and the meaning, is what 1st grade addition word problems are really testing. And here is the part nobody tells parents: almost every addition story a first-grader meets is one of just three kinds.

Learn to spot which of the three you are looking at, and the sum practically writes itself. Below are the three story types, a four-step method that fits on one hand, and worked examples kept within 20 the way the NCERT Grade 1 syllabus expects.

The three kinds of addition stories a six-year-old meets

Teachers have a name for these — problem structures — but your child does not need the jargon. They just need to hear enough of each type to recognise the shape of it.

1. Add-to stories (something joins the group)

Something starts, then more arrives. ‘Diya had 6 stickers. She earned 4 more.’ There is a clear before and after, and the group grows. These are the easiest to see as addition because the action — giving, earning, buying, arriving — feels like adding. Start here.

2. Put-together stories (two groups, one total)

Nothing moves; you are simply counting two groups at once. ‘There are 8 boys and 5 girls in the class. How many children altogether?’ Nobody joined anyone — the two groups already existed. Children who have only met add-to stories sometimes freeze here because there is no action word. Point out that ‘altogether’ and ‘in all’ are the tell.

3. Compare stories (how many more, put together)

This is the sneaky one. ‘Rahul has 9 laddoos. Meera has 4 more than Rahul. How many does Meera have?’ The words ‘more than’ often make a child subtract on reflex, but here you are building Meera’s total by adding her extra 4 to Rahul’s 9. I spend the most time on compare stories, because they are the ones that catch children out for years if the habit sets in early.

Read, underline, solve, check

Once the type is clear, a simple four-step routine keeps a child from rushing to a wrong answer. Say the steps out loud together until they become automatic.

  • Read the whole problem twice — once for the story, once for the numbers.
  • Underline the two numbers and the question word (how many, altogether, in all).
  • Solve by writing a number sentence: 7 + 5 = ___, not just a scribbled answer.
  • Check that the answer makes sense — is it bigger than both numbers? For addition it always should be.

That last check is the quiet hero. A child who has just added 7 and 5 and written 12 can glance back and confirm 12 is bigger than both 7 and 5, so an addition was reasonable. It catches the ‘more than means subtract’ slip before it lands on paper.

Worked examples within 20

Here are the three types side by side, each solved the same way. Notice the number sentence is identical in shape — only the story wrapper changes.

Story typeProblemNumber sentenceAnswer
Add-toAarav had 7 marbles; his sister gave 5 more7 + 5 = ___12 marbles
Put-together8 boys and 5 girls in the class, altogether?8 + 5 = ___13 children
CompareRahul has 9 laddoos; Meera has 4 more9 + 4 = ___13 laddoos

For the sums that cross ten — 7 + 5, 9 + 4 — lean on the make-ten strategy your child already uses in plain addition: turn 9 + 4 into 10 + 3. The word problem is only a costume; the arithmetic underneath is the same.

The mistake to watch for: keyword hunting

You will see it advised everywhere — ‘more’ means add, ‘left’ means subtract. It is a trap. In ‘Meera has 4 more than Rahul,’ the word ‘more’ sits inside an addition; in ‘How many more does she need?’ the same word points to subtraction. Keywords are a hint, never a rule. The reliable habit is the one above: work out what is actually happening in the story — is a group growing, are two groups being counted, is one amount being built from another — then choose the operation. Teach the structure, not the vocabulary shortcut.

Why the numbers stay small on purpose

Every example here keeps the sum at or below 20, and that is deliberate. In Grade 1 the reading and the reasoning are the hard part, not the calculation. If the numbers are big enough that a child struggles to add them, all their attention goes to the sum and none is left for understanding the story. Keep sums within 20 for a full term of word-problem practice before you push higher. There is no prize for rushing.

Try the quiz, then the printable practice

The eight-question quiz below mixes all three story types, all with sums within 20. Let your child read each one aloud, name the type, then pick an answer — and read the explanations together for any they miss. When they are ready for longer written practice, the printable word-problems e-book at the end gives graded story sums with a full answer key.

quiz.title: 1st Grade Addition Word Problems Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight short story problems mixing add-to, put-together and compare types, all with sums within 20. Read each one, decide the type, pick an answer, then press Check my score.

questions.q: Aarav had 7 marbles. His sister gave him 5 more. How many now?
questions.explanation: This is an add-to story: 7 + 5 = 12. Make ten if it helps: 7 + 5 becomes 10 + 2 = 12.

questions.q: There are 8 boys and 5 girls in a class. How many children altogether?
questions.explanation: A put-together story: count both groups. 8 + 5 = 13. The word ‘altogether’ tells you to add.

questions.q: Rahul has 9 laddoos. Meera has 4 more than Rahul. How many does Meera have?
questions.explanation: A compare story. ‘More than’ here builds Meera’s total: 9 + 4 = 13. Do not let ‘more’ trick you into subtracting.

questions.q: Diya earned 6 stickers, then earned 4 more. How many stickers now?
questions.explanation: Add-to story: 6 + 4 = 10. The two groups make a full ten.

questions.q: A basket has 5 red apples and 7 green apples. How many apples in all?
questions.explanation: Put-together: 5 + 7 = 12. ‘In all’ is the signal to add both groups.

questions.q: Which step should you do LAST when solving a word problem?
questions.explanation: Read, underline, solve, then check. Checking that the answer is bigger than both numbers catches mistakes.

questions.q: Sana has 8 pencils. Ravi has 3 more than Sana. How many does Ravi have?
questions.explanation: A compare story: build Ravi’s total by adding. 8 + 3 = 11.

questions.q: For any addition word problem, the answer should be…
questions.explanation: Adding makes the total grow, so a correct addition answer is bigger than each number you started with. That is the quick check.

faq.q: What are the three types of addition word problems in Grade 1?
faq.a: Add-to (something joins a group, like a gift arriving), put-together (two groups counted as one total, signalled by ‘altogether’ or ‘in all’), and compare (one amount is a few more than another). Naming the type first makes the sum obvious.

faq.q: Why does my child get word problems wrong even when their addition is fine?
faq.a: Because the hard part is reading, not adding. A child can know 7 + 5 = 12 yet not realise a story is asking for it. Teaching the story structures — and the read-underline-solve-check habit — fixes the gap.

faq.q: Are keyword tricks like ‘more means add’ reliable?
faq.a: No. ‘More’ sits inside additions and subtractions both — ‘4 more than Rahul’ is an addition, ‘how many more needed’ is a subtraction. Teach children to picture what happens in the story rather than hunt for a magic word.

faq.q: How large should the numbers be in Grade 1 word problems?
faq.a: Keep sums within 20 for the whole first year of practice. At this age the reading and reasoning are the challenge; small numbers let a child spend their attention on understanding the story, not on a hard calculation.
